messages.subject: Re: Using R/qtl on data with more than 2 alleles per locus
messages.subject_clean: Using R/qtl on data with more than 2 alleles per locus
messages.body_plain:
Hello Karl, the guys of the email, and everyone...
maybe this comment is a bit late.
I'm new in R/qtl and not an expert bioinformatics and R (not at all!!!). That's why I've used Joinmap and MapQTL for a long period. I share the opinion that they express in their email, R/qtl is great for QTL analysis because of its versatility.
I think is not so difficult to infer the loci phases since you work with joinmap in outbred crosses, as is a data that is calculated when constructing maps in that software. Also, since you construct paternal and maternal maps, you can have the genotypic data of the markers segregating for each parent, like a pseudo-testcross (create maternal and paternal nodes). Having phases and genotypes (in the pseudotestcross mode, two alleles assuming you work with a diploid species), you can transform genotypes in the RQTL format, using a simple logical function from Excel or alternative (sorry, I don't know to work in Perl): if the phase is "coupling" and the genotype is AB, let "AB", if "repulsion" then let "AA".
Although I can be losing some interaction effects between the four alleles, this worked to me for detect main QTLs in MQM mode...
Please if I'm wrong, let me know!!!
Cheers!
IgorPC

El lunes, 9 de mayo de 2016, 14:40:50 (UTC-3), Karl Broman escribió:
> I got the following email, and I though it and my response might be of interest.
>
> > After perusing "A brief Tour of R/qtl" and trying out the examples within, we are highly impressed by R/qtl's functionality.
> > In particular, it is much faster than the softwares we are currently using (JoinMap & MapQTL from Kyazama), and also much more versatile.
> > Hence, we wish to apply R/qtl to our future projects.
> > However, one obstacle we have encountered is that R/qtl seems to assume that there are only 2 alleles (hence 3 genotypes i.e. AA, Aa, aa) per locus, but this is not true for our data.
> > The markers we use include SSRs and SNPs. Most SSRs, and even some SNPs, have more than 2 alleles per locus.
> > Also, while it is possible to specially breed a mapping population with only 2 alleles per locus, this is highly impractical for some species, especially those with a long life cycle.
> > Is there a way to use R/qtl on data with more than 2 alleles per locus?
> > Any advice or help you can provide will be highly appreciated!
>
> R/qtl focuses on simple crosses between inbred lines.
>
>
> If you have a large sibship derived from two outbred individuals, it's *possible* to analyze it in R/qtl using the cross type "4way", for a phase-known 4-way cross (the 4 being the grandparents), but you first have to infer phase in the parents, which is usually hard, and there's little documentation.
>
>
> There still aren't many options for QTL mapping in outbred crosses, unfortunately.
>
>
> Alternatively, you could do association mapping (for example, perform analysis of variance at each SNP) using something like PLINK.
>
> karl
>

I would like to thank you for your previous advice. They helped me a lot. But I have two other questions…

W dniu wtorek, 29 sierpnia 2017 16:35:13 UTC+2 użytkownik Karl Broman napisał:
> If you ensure that the two crosses have the same markers in the same order, you could use ripple() on a given chromosome with each cross, and then sum either the LOD scores of the crossover counts.
>
>   rip1 <- ripple(cross1, method="countxo", chr=3, window=7)
>   rip2 <- ripple(cross2, method="countxo", chr=3, window=7)
>   rip <- rip1
>   rip[,"obligXO"] <- rip1[,"obligXO"] + rip2[,"obligXO"]
>   summary(rip)
>
> or for the likelihood method:
>
>   rip1 <- ripple(cross1, method="likelihood", chr=3, window=4)
>   rip2 <- ripple(cross2, method="likelihood", chr=3, window=4)
>   rip <- rip1
>   rip[,"LOD"] <- rip1[,"LOD"] + rip2[,"LOD"]
>   summary(rip)
>
> Alternatively, if you're willing to assume that the recombination rates are the same in the two crosses, you could combine your two 4-way cross objects into one and build the map using the two crosses combined.
>
> karl
>

I used the same primers to analyze both mapping populations and I would like to present ‘common’ linkages (which is one of my tasks). For this purpose, I created two separate maps, which in the next step, I wanted to combine into one (how to do it, I dont't know yet ☹). If it is possible to receive such a common map at once, I would like to kindly ask you for some advice how can I do this?

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] df for t test of additive and dominance effect
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] df for t test of additive and dominance effect
messages.body_plain:
Degrees of freedom concerns the estimated residual SD, which would be number of individuals minus number of parameters estimated. In this context, it's generally so large that it doesn't really matter.

karl

> On Sep 3, 2017, at 10:28 PM, Mingzi Xu <xu4...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I estimated coefficients for additive and dominance effect for each QTL in a multiple QTL model with fitqtl(). The summary gives a t value for each estimate. I'd like to know the p value for each t test but I'm a little confused about the df. Should it be # of individual - # of parameters estimated -1? I'm also not clear on how additive and dominance effect are counted in the model, whether they represent independent estimates in the model or one is derived from another. In the former case # of parameters estimated = # of QTL main and interaction terms but in the latter case, it's twice that number, right? Could you please help me?
>
> For example, if the following results are from a sample of 100 individuals, the final model contains 3 QTL and no interaction term (i.e., formula = Q1+Q2+Q3), what is the df for each estimate?
>
> Estimated effects:
>
> -----------------
>

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] df for t test of additive and dominance effect
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] df for t test of additive and dominance effect
messages.body_plain:
Yes, Bonferroni correction is generally quite conservative. And you really should consider the full model search and not just the set of loci that you arrived at in the end...much more than 7 tests, I mean.

In studying the additive and dominance effects, d=0 is interesting as corresponding to no dominance, and d = +/- a is interesting as corresponding to fully dominant. But the latter would require you to take account of the correlation between the estimates. Best to fit the dominant model and compare it to the full model, though there is no function to do this in R/qtl.

Personally, I think alleles won't be exactly additive or exactly dominant/recessive, and so I prefer not to use the statistical tests which answer a yes/no question about the effects. Rather, I'd just look at the estimates themselves.

karl

messages.subject: Confidence interval estimation for multiple QTL models
messages.subject_clean: Confidence interval estimation for multiple QTL models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Broman,

I have a few questions regarding estimating the confidence intervals.

The first question is rather basic. By definition, the 1.5-LOD support interval is the interval whose boundaries has LOD score 1.5 unit lower than the maximum. But if the nearest marker or simulated locus is beyond 1.5 LOD away from the peak, the interval we actually get is more than 1.5-LOD support. In the example below, the LOD drop is way beyond 1.5 unit, I think due to the the peak rising sharply (see attached figure). Also, we can imagine the sharper the peak arises, the more units the actual LOD drop from the peak there would be. Then does this create a problem of interpretability, i.e., interval widths for different peaks are not actually all the same LOD support level. What should we do about this situation? Should we simply report the interval as the "1.5"-LOD support interval assuming everyone would understand that it sometimes is more than 1.5-LOD support (which is a little unfair to super sharp peaks) or should we try to simulate genotype at a finer grid size?

In your book, it says that the Bayes CI has consistent coverage so may be preferred over the 1.5 or 1.8-LOD support interval. And later in the book, it says that how the two methods behave for multiple QTL model is not well understood. I'm wondering what is your opinion on the two methods for multiple QTL models. Is there one we should prefer?

My last question is that when I estimate the Bayes interval for multiple QTL models, I sometimes got an interval of width 0 (see the example below). A confidence interval of 0 cM may sound like a good news but I'm not sure if this is a sign of problematic, overly optimistic performance of the Bayes estimate. Do you have experience with this situation? Can I trust this result?

Sorry for my many question and I really appreciate your opinion!

> lodint(qtl4c.9.m.refine6,1.5,qtl.index=5)

           chr pos      lod

c5.loc27     5  27 150.8491

messages.body_plain:
> The first question is rather basic. By definition, the 1.5-LOD support interval is the interval whose boundaries has LOD score 1.5 unit lower than the maximum. But if the nearest marker or simulated locus is beyond 1.5 LOD away from the peak, the interval we actually get is more than 1.5-LOD support. In the example below, the LOD drop is way beyond 1.5 unit, I think due to the the peak rising sharply (see attached figure). Also, we can imagine the sharper the peak arises, the more units the actual LOD drop from the peak there would be. Then does this create a problem of interpretability, i.e., interval widths for different peaks are not actually all the same LOD support level. What should we do about this situation? Should we simply report the interval as the "1.5"-LOD support interval assuming everyone would understand that it sometimes is more than 1.5-LOD support (which is a little unfair to super sharp peaks) or should we try to simulate genotype at a finer grid size?

The end points of the interval are always at positions where you calculated the LOD score, which is determined by the 'step' argument in calc.genoprob or sim.geno. If the LOD curve is dropping rapidly, you may want use a smaller value for step and calculate the LOD curve at a more dense set of positions.

> In your book, it says that the Bayes CI has consistent coverage so may be preferred over the 1.5 or 1.8-LOD support interval. And later in the book, it says that how the two methods behave for multiple QTL model is not well understood. I'm wondering what is your opinion on the two methods for multiple QTL models. Is there one we should prefer?

The LOD support intervals are easier to explain, but the approximate Bayes intervals have appeared to be better behaved. But we really don't know much about their performance in the context of multiple-QTL models. I'm not willing to state a strong preference. And I generally don't put much trust in them.

> My last question is that when I estimate the Bayes interval for multiple QTL models, I sometimes got an interval of width 0 (see the example below). A confidence interval of 0 cM may sound like a good news but I'm not sure if this is a sign of problematic, overly optimistic performance of the Bayes estimate. Do you have experience with this situation? Can I trust this result?

We're approximately the Bayes posterior by a set of rectangles centered at each position where you calculated the LOD score. If the LOD score is extremely large and drops dramatically in the region, it can end up that a single position is estimated to have 95% posterior. I would use a finer grid in this case, to get the interval to cover more than one pseudomarker. And I generally use expandtomarkers=TRUE.

karl
